results.title: [SMM Analysis] Price Hikes Reach Desktop Devices; Computing Power Shortage Shows No Sign of Peaking - Shanghai Metals Market (SMM)
highlights:
This week, the computing power hardware market saw simultaneous shifts on both the supply and demand sides. On the demand side, the price-increase signal traveled down the transmission chain to the very end: monthly rental for 5090 eight-card servers in east China rose from 13,500 yuan/unit/month in early September to 16,000 yuan/unit/month, an increase of 18.5%. Rental prices and desktop AI device procurement prices moved up in tandem, cross-validating the growth and transmission of computing power demand. SMM believes this round of shortage has evolved from a one-way pattern of "demand transmitting down the chain" into a two-way squeeze of "demand pressing down while capacity pulls up.

...

In SMM's original analysis of computing power rental prices published in August (https://news.smm.cn/news/OUOCOCJSCPBTL4VHB4H5A33TSPBACMIPBRZWDVI), the transmission effect of computing power rental prices had already become evident. The rental price of 5090 eight-card servers, located at the very end of the computing power rental price transmission chain, is a key indicator reflecting shifts in the supply-demand relationship of the computing power rental supply chain. In the week following the end of China's 2026 National Day holiday, unusual movement occurred at the very end of the chain. SMM market tracking shows that on October 10, the rental price of 5090 servers in east China rose to 16,000 yuan/unit/month, up 18.5% from 13,500 yuan/unit/month in early September, reflecting the current undersupply in the 5090 rental market.

...

At this point, the growth and transmission of computing power demand have been confirmed by two independent price lines: in the rental market, the 5090 monthly rental and single-card prices have continued to rise, measuring the supply and demand of existing computing power; in the desktop equipment market, the purchase prices of AI terminals such as DGX Spark have risen, measuring the intensity of new computing power demand. The price increases in the two markets belong to different contract forms, but they point in the same direction.

...

Since August, the SMM computing power rental price composite index (average price, yuan per card per hour) has shown a "three-stage" rise, with a total increase of about 26%.

The index pattern corroborates the spot signals from SMM market tracking: the stage high at the end of August corresponds to the first wave of high-end computing power price increases being transmitted to the mid-end, the September consolidation corresponds to the "buffer absorption" stage, and the jump after October is synchronized with first-line collection signals such as an 18.5% rise in monthly rent for east China 5090 eight-card servers, an 8%–9% rise in 5090 single-card prices over three weeks, and a 13% rise in DGX Spark channel prices over three weeks—after the buffer layer was breached, the shortage has become explicit at the index level.

The computing power demand for training and inference of the new generation of large models is first transmitted to the GB300 and B300 series; top-performance servers are expensive and supply is constrained, so demand spills over in turn to the H200, H100, and existing second-hand A100 series, then down to the Pro 6000 and 5090, and finally to the 4090. SMM's judgment in August was that "the mid-end computing power rental supply side has a buffer, and subsequent price transmission lacks momentum"; two months later, the buffer has been breached—the Pro 6000 server version single-card spot price in south China has risen from about 130,000 yuan in August (third-party market data) to 182,000 yuan in late September and early October (according to SMM), an increase of about 40%. The 5090 and Pro 6000, which took over the price increases from the upper tier, have themselves become scarce models: the computing power rental demand borne by these two devices, especially inference demand, continues to be transmitted downward after supply at that tier peaks.

...

Price fluctuations caused by reallocating capacity based on product profitability have already played out once in the memory industry. In 2023, when DRAM was in severe oversupply, Samsung joined production cuts and reduced its DRAM production plans, while announcing on its July 27 earnings call that "HBM high-bandwidth memory capacity dedicated to data center GPUs will at least double in 2024 compared with 2023." Three years later in 2026, LPDDR5X memory used in desktop devices and GDDR7 memory used in high-end consumer and workstation graphics cards are both weighed down by insufficient DRAM capacity supply, driving noticeable increases in whole-device prices—NVIDIA's two DGX Spark price hikes during the year and the launch of a 64GB memory version after the 128GB version are examples of system makers protecting margins amid rising memory prices.

...

This shows that limited chip capacity always flows to the category with higher unit returns; and from capacity strategy adjustment to supply-demand relationship changes taking effect and triggering price movements, there is a two-to-three-year time lag. In addition, the availability of vacant server rental resources and the reluctance of advanced computing equipment holders to sell have amplified downstream the hardware procurement price and computing power rental price increases caused by the above supply-demand imbalance.

...

From the supply side: Nvidia's annual chip architecture iteration, combined with proactive product mix adjustments, means the GPU market is almost always in the capacity ramp-up period of some generation. And the discontinuation of the 5090 shows that supply contraction takes not only the form of "insufficient capacity" but also "capacity reallocation": when total capacity is constrained by memory and other factors, producers will allocate limited wafer and VRAM quotas to the product lines with the highest unit returns, and consumer-grade graphics cards are being systematically downgraded on this priority list. Another signal from the supply side comes from changes in the internal division of labor at telecom operators: the core work of intelligent computing managers at various branches has shifted from maintaining customer relationships to securing the GPU server supply chain and ensuring on-time, on-quantity equipment delivery—the functions of sales-oriented and procurement-oriented roles are further merging.

results.title: AI compute crunch deepens as chip rental costs jump 60% and rivals scramble for power
highlights:
- A desperate scramble for AI computing power is upending Silicon Valley, the WSJ reports, with chip rental costs up 60% in a year, rivals forced into unlikely alliances and startups squeezed by multiyear contracts and upfront fees of up to 30%.

The squeeze hands pricing power to anyone who already controls chips, data centres and electricity, favouring hyperscalers, neoclouds and chipmakers over the startups trying to rent from them. Rising rental prices and tougher contract terms point to stronger near-term revenue for compute providers, but also to growing concentration risk, as only the biggest and best-funded labs can lock in capacity. The rush to overbook capacity as a hedge raises the danger of a sharp reversal if demand disappoints, leaving firms stuck with costly lease commitments and a glut of resold capacity. That fragility echoes recent warnings that financing, power and data centre delays, not demand, are now the binding constraints on the AI build-out.

...

- A shortage of computing power is driving a frantic, industry-wide scramble across Silicon Valley, with power struggles inside companies and unlikely alliances between rivals, the Wall Street Journal (gated) reported
- The cost of renting Nvidia H100 chips on a one-year contract has risen 60% in the past year, according to research firm SemiAnalysis
- Cloud providers now demand multiyear contracts with upfront payments often as high as 30%, sometimes backed by guarantors, shutting out many smaller players
- Top executives are personally brokering deals, including Anthropic’s agreement to lease more than 300 megawatts from SpaceX, reported to be worth up to $45 billion
- Announced capacity often fails to materialise, with projects delayed, cancelled or scaled back, and some deals collapsing when data centres slip
- Venture firms are now reserving GPU clusters for their portfolio companies, as access to compute rivals capital as the key constraint for startups

...

Compute, the industry’s shorthand for computing power, has become the AI boom’s most coveted resource, and there is not enough of it. The squeeze is showing up in prices. The hourly cost of renting computing power from Nvidia’s H100 chips on a one-year contract has jumped 60% in the past year, according to research firm SemiAnalysis. Alphabet expects capital spending of up to $200 billion this year, much of it on AI infrastructure.

...

For smaller players, the terms are becoming punishing. Where startups could once rent chips flexibly, cloud providers now require multiyear contracts with upfront payments often as high as 30%, sometimes backed by guarantors. Some are turning in desperation to providers with weaker security or infrastructure. Much of the capacity that has been promised is not yet available, with projects delayed, cancelled or scaled back. One open-source startup lost a capacity deal when its partner’s data centre was delayed.

results.title: Power, Not HBM, Is AI's Real Bottleneck, Nvidia Partner Says - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights:
GMI Cloud, a key neocloud partner of Nvidia, has identified electricity as the biggest obstacle to the spread of artificial intelligence and said it will increase investment in Asia. The company believes conflicts over securing power are intensifying in the United States, while Asia is moving faster to build sovereign AI.

Alex Yeh, chief executive officer of GMI Cloud, told The Seoul Economic Daily at the company's Mountain View headquarters in the United States on the 5th of this month that electricity is a more fundamental bottleneck than high-bandwidth memory (HBM). HBM can be obtained on the spot market by paying a premium, the CEO explained, but power requires transformers and transmission grid facilities to back it up, and building one's own power plant is easily blocked by opposition from local communities and political circles. Yeh said data center disputes in the United States lead to supply chain delays, while the burden is relatively lighter in Asia. The CEO also cited the ability to raise funds through Japan at half the cost of competitors as a strength.

...

GMI Cloud is one of Nvidia's seven major neocloud partners and receives priority supply of the latest graphics processing units (GPUs). It operates data centers in the United States, Thailand and Malaysia, and has decided to build a $500 million data center in Taiwan. In Kagoshima, Japan, it plans to invest $12 billion to establish a 1-gigawatt AI factory. The latest Nvidia GPUs to be installed at the two sites total about 9,000 units. Taiwanese media point to Yeh being the son of Yeh Chia-wen, chairman of Hongyi International and a co-founder of Realtek, as the reason behind the company's rapid local partnerships.

results.title: GPU price index explained: list prices, marketplace medians and transaction indices — AI Compute Radar
highlights:
GPU rental prices now have indices, announced futures and prediction markets of their own. Behind the word “price” sit three different numbers: what a provider posts, what a marketplace offers, and what renters actually paid. This page says which is which, who publishes what, and where the numbers on this site fit.

...

## Three kinds of GPU price

01

### List price

The hourly rate a provider posts for an instance or a GPU, before any discount.

Examples

RunPod's posted on-demand price; the AWS, Azure and Oracle Cloud price lists.

Good for

Exact and reproducible: anyone can read the same number from the same page.

Blind spot

Moves rarely and says nothing about discounts, reserved terms or whether capacity is free.

### Marketplace median

The middle of the offers a renter could take at one moment on an open marketplace, with the number of offers behind it.

Examples

Vast.ai and Clore.ai, read every hour on this site.

Good for

Moves with supply and demand within hours, and the offer count shows how thin the market is.

Blind spot

An offer is not a deal: it shows what was asked, not what was paid, and a median over a handful of offers is fragile.

03

### Transaction index

A daily rate computed from rentals that were actually executed, usually weighted by volume and cleaned of outliers.

Examples

Ornn's Compute Price Index describes itself this way; Silicon Data standardises observations from many sources into one daily rate.

Good for

Closest to what compute really changed hands for, which is why futures reference such indices.

Blind spot

Needs access to deal data, so the inputs cannot be checked from outside, and a blended rate hides which provider moved.

...

- Launched the Silicon Data H100 Rental Index (Bloomberg ticker SDH100RT) on 20 May 2025: a daily rate built from 3.5 million pricing data points across rental platforms.
- Standardises each observation for machine specification, rental terms and location, and publishes separate neocloud and hyperscaler readings.
- CME Group announced the Silicon Data H100 and B200 Rental Index Futures on 11 August 2026: listed on NYMEX, each contract a month's worth of rent for one GPU, planned for 5 October 2026 pending regulatory review.

...

- We publish what each source shows, one source at a time: marketplace medians with their offer counts and quartiles, RunPod's posted floor and the big clouds' list prices, read hourly or four times a day, each with its timestamp.
- We never blend sources into one rate and never compute a transaction index: we see offers and price lists, not deals.
- The Rent Index says what each source's daily median did over 7 to 90 days. It describes; it does not forecast.
- Two derived numbers sit beside the readings. The cloud premium divides the cheapest big-cloud list price by the same day's marketplace median for the same card, so a reader sees what a reserved instance cost against one marketplace GPU that day. Market depth shows how many offers stood behind each day's median, and a median over fewer than five offers is flagged as a thin market.
- Our series are not designed or offered as a reference rate for settling financial contracts, and nothing here is investment advice.

results.title: Your 32GB Card, Gone: 41% Memory Hike | AIChieve
highlights:
Nvidia has reportedly stopped making the only consumer graphics card with 32 gigabytes (GB) of video memory [1]. That silicon is going to professional boards instead. Nine days earlier, on 1 October, the discount cloud firm Nebius raised its pay-as-you-go rental rates for the second time in three months. Its largest increase, 41%, landed on memory rather than on compute [3]. Neither move is about raw speed. In both, what is scarce and what sets the price is memory space.

...

On 10 October, Tom’s Hardware reported that Nvidia has stopped supplying the GB202 chip to makers of consumer cards. That is the die inside the 5090. The outlet cited a leaked factory notice, plus a second hardware leaker who said future supply of the die is reserved for data-center and professional cards [1].

...

- 84 GB vs 32 GB — Same core count: the professional card Nvidia listed in September carries about 2.6 times the video memory of the consumer card it shares a core count with. Nvidia has published no price for it [1][2].
- 41% — The memory line: Nebius lifted its rate on memory from 1 October, against 17% to 21% on graphics chips and 25% on some processor-only instances. Its 96 GB workstation tier did not move at all [3][4].
- $4,999 for 64 GB — The desk box inversion: Nvidia’s new half-size Spark machine ships on 23 October “starting at $4,999”. The 128 GB model that “launched at $3999 about a year ago” now lists at $6,950 [5].
- $3.47 — The H100 hour: that was the median on-demand rental across 41 providers in the week of 5 October, up 4.0% in four weeks and 16% in a year, even as the premium the big cloud firms charge narrowed to 75% [6].

...

First, the halt is a leak, not a statement. Nvidia has not confirmed it, has disputed it in private to at least one outlet, and cards already built can keep selling for a while [1]. The half I can stand behind is the pricing above it.

Second, renting has not closed. A one-year reservation still runs about 32% below on-demand, and a three-year about 49%. Spot capacity sits near 59% of the on-demand rate [6]. A team that will tie up capital, or put up with jobs dying mid-run, can still move its number down.

Third, the rises are not universal. Of 22 rental models tracked this year, 14 went up and 8 fell, and the 96 GB workstation tier did not move [4][6]. What repriced is memory-heavy gear, which is the same thing Nvidia is re-cutting its silicon to carry more of. TrendForce’s numbers from August, before this window, already had memory at 68% of major cloud providers’ capital spending for 2027, from 47% this year [8].
